## Simple explanation

A confusion matrix shows how often a classifier predicts each class
compared with the known labels. It makes types of classification errors
visible instead of summarizing them in a single score.

## Technical explanation

For binary classification, the matrix contains true positives, false
positives, true negatives, and false negatives. These counts can be used
to calculate precision, recall, specificity, and accuracy. In multiclass
tasks, a matrix records counts for each actual and predicted class.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Different mistakes can have different consequences. A confusion matrix
helps engineers understand which classes are confused and whether the
model's errors are acceptable for a particular application.

## How it works

For each labeled example, compare the predicted label with its reference
label and increment the corresponding cell. Always check the axis order:
libraries may display actual labels in rows and predictions in columns,
or the reverse.

In the diagram below, **ostrich is the positive class**. Rows are actual
labels and columns are predicted labels.

## Practical example

For our penguin-versus-ostrich classifier, the matrix can show how many
penguin images were predicted as ostrich and how many ostrich images were
predicted as penguin. The [binary-classification notebook](../../notebooks/B/binary-classification.ipynb)
includes a prompt to inspect these errors.

## Common misconceptions

- A confusion matrix does not explain why a prediction was wrong.
- A matrix of counts can obscure class imbalance; also inspect normalized
  rates when useful.
- A high diagonal count can coexist with poor performance on a small but
  important class.
